Flexicap Funds: 5-Star Rated by Value Research (August 2026) 📊 FinAlpha1Pager

We analysed ₹1.19 Lakh Cr across HDFC, Bank of India, and ITI Flexicap to see where strategies align and where they split.

Key takeaways from the side-by-side comparison:

🚀 Benchmark Outperformance:
 • Bank of India and ITI beat the Nifty 500 TRI across all three timeframes (3M, 6M, and 1Y).
 • ITI delivered the highest alpha over 6M (+19.1%) and 1Y (+11.2% vs. benchmark’s -2.0%), whereas giant HDFC lagged behind the benchmark over 6M (+6.1%) and 1Y (-2.8%).

🏦 Cash Cushions & Asset Mix:
 • Bank of India carries a notable 11.0% debt cushion to navigate volatility and preserve liquidity.
 • HDFC and ITI run higher equity deployments (94.8% and 93.4%), with HDFC holding a 2.2% allocation in REITs & InvITs and ITI maintaining 3.0% in cash.

📊 Market Cap Allocation:
 • HDFC anchors heavily in mega caps with a 74% large-cap tilt (only 10% in small caps). 
 • Bank of India and ITI take a much more aggressive broader-market stance, allocating 39% and 31% directly to small caps.

🤝 Consensus vs. Differentiators:

 • Consensus: ICICI Bank and SBI are held across all three funds, while HDFC Bank, Bharti Airtel, and L&T appear across two.

 • HDFC Differentiator: High conviction in frontline banking and large caps led by Axis Bank (6.2%), Eternal (3.4%), Kotak Mahindra Bank (3.3%), and SBI Life (3.2%). 

• Bank of India Differentiator: High-alpha mid/small-cap manufacturing and consumption bets led by HAL (3.0%), Sky Gold (2.9%), Quality Power (2.8%), and Balrampur Chini (2.8%).

 • ITI Differentiator: Blends mega-cap weights like Reliance (3.7%) with unique bets in new-age tech and niche engineering via Ather Energy (2.1%), Aditya Infotech (2.1%), and Apar Industries (1.8%).

WAKE UP SID (2009) was released 17 years ago today.🎬

The film is a coming-of-age romance drama that tells the story of Siddharth "Sid" Mehra, an aimless, spoiled college graduate. After failing his exams, Sid finds his purpose, career, and love through a hardworking writer named Aisha. The film was directed by Ayan Mukerji starring Bollywood's Superstar #RanbirKapoor, Konkona Sen Sharma in lead roles alongside Anupam Kher, Supriya Pathak in supporting roles.

The film was the 14th highest-grossing film of the year, collecting a nett of ₹27.94 cr and ₹47.10 cr worldwide against its ₹18 cr budget, becoming a Semi-Hit at the box office. However, over time, it achieved a massive cult status after its release on television and digital platforms, it became a favourite coming-of-age film for millions of youth across India. Even today's youth connect with the film regarding their life and career confusion. the film had such a deep impact on youth and teenagers that, at the time, people used to put up photos and posters of RK (Sid) inside their cupboards and on their room walls. 💯

Ranbir Kapoor proved he is not just a chocolate boy hero but a very fine actor. His performance as Sid remains one of his finest, earning him the Filmfare Award for Best Actor (Critics), while Ayan Mukerji won the Best Debut Director award for his very first film. Additionally, Kavita Seth won the Best Female Playback Singer award for the soulful song "Iktara". The film's title track, "Wake Up Sid", remains incredibly popular among the youth even today, delivering a unique, super hit freshness and vibe. ❤️

Golden Retrievers look like sunshine with a tail… but underneath all that fluff is a professional retriever, part-time comedian, and full-time emotional support roommate.

Here are 10 things you may not know about Goldens - with a little Peach Cat commentary, because apparently Biscuit requested supervision.

1. They were developed in Scotland in the 1800s, bred to retrieve game from both land and water. Peach: “So the obsession with carrying random objects is technically a résumé skill.”

2. Their famously gentle “soft mouth” was encouraged so they could retrieve without damaging what they carried. Some can even hold surprisingly delicate objects.

3. Goldens often stay puppy-like for YEARS. The body grows up. The goofy little brain sometimes misses the memo.

4. That gorgeous coat is a water-resistant double coat designed for outdoor work. Translation: rain rolls off… but somehow the fur still ends up on everything you own.

5. Retrieving is deeply wired into them. Socks, shoes, toys, towels—if Biscuit proudly delivers something nobody asked for, he considers the mission successful.

6. They’re regularly used as guide, therapy, assistance, search-and-rescue and detection dogs because they tend to combine intelligence with an eagerness to work with people.

7. Goldens are surprisingly athletic. Behind the sweet face is a dog built for swimming, running and spending approximately nine hours convincing you to throw the ball “one more time.”

8. There are noticeable American, British and Canadian Golden Retriever styles, with differences in build, coat and coloring-even though they’re all the same breed.

9. They’re famous for being social, but that sweetness also means many Goldens REALLY want to be included. Bathroom trip? Congratulations, you now have security.

10. And maybe the most Golden Retriever thing of all: they were bred to bring things back to people… and somehow generations later, they’re still happiest when they’re bringing us something.

A ball. A sock. A stick. A little chaos.

Or, on the days we need it most, comfort.

Peach’s official verdict: Golden Retrievers are basically sunshine that learned how to shed.

Biscuit disagrees.

He says it’s “sparkle.”

An unnamed hyperscaler just committed ~₹11,400 cr to a Pune cable company. For five years.

The company is Sterlite Tech. Nvidia sells the GPUs and someone has to wire tens of thousands of them together inside an AI data centre. 

That's optical connectivity, and STL just signed a ~USD 1.2 bn LTSA to supply it from CY26 to CY30. One contract, ~2.4x its entire FY26 revenue of ₹4,745 cr. Five years to execute, but demand locked till 2030 📡

Order book was ₹18,618 cr in June. Since then: ~$210 mn, ~$288 mn, ₹960 cr and now this. 

One question: May's ~$1.11 bn worth of product award letter (PAL) was also from "a hyperscale partner". Today's signed contract could be that deal maturing in the shape of an Long Term Supply Agreement (LTSA) instead of a fresh one. 

Either way, a ₹4,745 cr revenue company sits on 5–7x that in orders

Every AI data centre is a web of fibre. The picks and shovels found their buyers.

Reading a Concall, Following the Supply Chain: A Small Texmaco to  Ramkrishna Forgings Connection

One thing I enjoy about reading concalls is that sometimes a small operational comment in one company leads you to another company and gives you a better picture of the industry.

While going through Texmaco Rail's Q1 FY27 concall, I came across a discussion around wheelsets.

Management said that industry production of wheels had been relatively subdued and that Texmaco remains dependent on the Rail Wheel Factory for part of its requirement. At the same time, management clarified that it currently had enough stock and alternative sourcing avenues for its private and export orders, and therefore did not expect a wheelset constraint in the immediate quarters.

That made me curious about the broader wheel supply chain.

A wagon cannot be completed and delivered without critical components such as wheels/wheelsets. 

So even when a wagon manufacturer has a large order book and manufacturing capacity, availability of critical components can influence how quickly that order book gets converted into physical deliveries.

And this is where I came across the Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh Rail Systems wheel project.

The important point here is that I am not suggesting Ramkrishna Forgings is setting up this plant specifically to solve Texmaco's wheelset shortage.
Its current disclosed orders are primarily linked to passenger trains, locomotives and other railway requirements.

The interesting connection is much broader.

India has historically depended significantly on imports for forged railway wheels. 

In 2022–23, the government said around 80,000 forged wheels worth approximately Rs 520 crore were being imported, and at the same time highlighted the need to increase domestic manufacturing capacity as railway wheel demand was expected to rise.

The government subsequently opened the space for private players to build domestic wheel-manufacturing capacity.

Ramkrishna Forgings, together with Titagarh Rail Systems, is now building a forged-wheel facility with planned capacity of around 2.28 lakh wheels per year, with project investment of roughly Rs 2,000 crore.

The project has now moved beyond just an announcement. Ramkrishna Forgings has said that trial production has started, with initial samples submitted to Indian Railways. It has also disclosed an order for around 80,000 wheels from Indian Railways, with additional requirements linked to the JV partner.

So the interesting observation for me isn't:
Ramkrishna Forgings will solve Texmaco's wheelset problem.

I don't think the available data supports that conclusion.

The more interesting observation is: Indian Railways has a large and growing requirement for railway wheels, historically relied partly on imports, has been dependent on a limited domestic supply ecosystem, and is now allowing private players to add significant domestic capacity.

That tells us something about the underlying demand-supply situation in the railway component ecosystem.

And when you put that back into Texmaco, the picture becomes clearer.

Texmaco ended Q1 FY27 with an order book of around Rs 9,923 crore, including more than 6,000 freight cars in the freight-car order book. Yet it delivered only around 1,054 freight cars during Q1.

Management has indicated that it has significant manufacturing capacity, but actual production can be affected by the availability of critical components and other execution constraints.

So there are really two separate questions:

1. Is there demand for railway rolling stock?
The large order books across the ecosystem suggest there is significant demand.

2. Can the supply chain add enough capacity to convert that demand into physical production?

This is where investments in wheels, bogies, components and other railway equipment become interesting.

The Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh project is therefore useful to me not because it directly fixes Texmaco's problem, but because it is another data point showing that the railway ecosystem itself needs additional domestic manufacturing capacity for critical components.

And this is also why I find reading across companies more useful than looking at one company in isolation.

A comment in a Texmaco concall about wheel availability led me to Ramkrishna Forgings' wheel project, which then led me back to the broader question of Indian Railways' wheel demand, domestic capacity and the government's push to bring in private manufacturing.

There is still a lot more to verify here, especially around actual wheel demand, capacity utilisation, qualification timelines and how much of the new capacity ultimately gets absorbed.

But the broader point is : 

When an industry has strong rolling-stock demand and critical component capacity is being expanded by new private players, it can indicate that the constraint is shifting from "is there demand?" to "how quickly can the ecosystem build enough capacity to fulfil it?"

That's the connection I found interesting while going through the Texmaco concall. Not a direct company-to-company link, but a useful way of understanding the railway supply chain.

🚨 KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK JUMPS OVER 3%: RBI APPROVES ANUP KUMAR SAHA AS NEW MD & CEO

Kotak Mahindra Bank shares rallied sharply on October 1 after the private-sector lender announced Anup Kumar Saha as its next Managing Director and CEO, providing clarity on one of the bank's biggest near-term uncertainties: leadership succession.

The stock rose more than 3% in morning trade and was trading around ₹431.20 at 10:18 AM.

THE BIG ANNOUNCEMENT 🏦

🔹 New MD & CEO: Anup Kumar Saha
🔹 RBI approval received
🔹 Term: 3 years
🔹 Effective from: January 1, 2027
🔹 Succeeds: Ashok Vaswani
🔹 Vaswani's current term ends: December 31, 2026
🔹 Shareholder approval will also be sought

The appointment provides a defined succession path after Vaswani decided not to seek another term.

WHO IS ANUP KUMAR SAHA? 👤

Saha joined Kotak Mahindra Bank in January 2026 and currently serves as Whole-Time Director and Executive Director.

At Kotak, he oversees:

🔹 Retail Banking
🔹 Government Business
🔹 Data Analytics
🔹 Marketing

But his previous experience is particularly interesting.

Before joining Kotak, Saha spent more than seven years at Bajaj Finance and eventually became its Managing Director & CEO.

He also spent around 14 years at ICICI Bank in senior leadership roles.

Overall, Saha brings more than three decades of professional experience, with deep exposure to consumer finance, retail banking, analytics and digital transformation.

THE BAJAJ FINANCE CONNECTION 📊

Saha joined Bajaj Finance in 2017 as President of Consumer Finance and subsequently served in several senior positions, including:

🔹 Deputy CEO
🔹 Executive Director
🔹 Deputy Managing Director
🔹 Managing Director & CEO

Kotak had highlighted earlier that during his tenure at Bajaj Finance, Saha played a significant role in scaling the consumer-finance franchise, digital transformation and customer-focused growth.

WHY THE MARKET IS WATCHING THIS CLOSELY 👀

Leadership succession had become an important overhang for Kotak Mahindra Bank.

When Vaswani announced in June that he would not seek reappointment, Kotak shares fell more than 2% as investors assessed the uncertainty around his successor.

The RBI's approval of an internal candidate now removes a major part of that uncertainty.

Importantly, Saha isn't joining Kotak from outside on January 1.

He is already part of the bank's senior leadership team and has been overseeing major customer-facing businesses, potentially allowing for a smoother transition.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

The significance of this announcement goes beyond today's 3% stock move.

Kotak Mahindra Bank is moving from succession uncertainty to a clearly defined leadership transition.

Saha's background also provides clues about areas that could remain important under his leadership:

Retail banking, customer acquisition, digital transformation, analytics and execution.

However, the appointment itself doesn't change Kotak's fundamentals overnight.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

The bigger questions will be how Kotak performs under the transition across:

🔹 Deposit growth
🔹 Loan growth
🔹 CASA franchise
🔹 Net interest margins
🔹 Retail banking
🔹 Digital customer acquisition
🔹 Asset quality
🔹 Return on equity
🔹 Execution of the bank's existing strategy

For investors tracking the banking sector, leadership uncertainty at Kotak has now reduced considerably.

The next phase will be about execution.

🇮🇳 INDIA’S #AI INFRASTRUCTURE CYCLE IS MUCH BROADER THAN IT LOOKS

India is often viewed as having limited direct exposure to the global AI boom because it has relatively few listed companies that design GPUs or build hyperscale AI platforms.

But the more important opportunity may sit one layer below AI applications — in the physical infrastructure required to run AI.

A bottom-up screen of ~1,800 Indian listed companies identifies 42 companies across power, data centres and semiconductors that are positioned as AI infrastructure enablers.

Together, these companies represent roughly US$670bn of listed market capitalisation, spanning large, mid, small and micro caps. The group includes 21 capital-goods companies, highlighting how much of the AI investment cycle ultimately flows into physical infrastructure.

THE AI INFRASTRUCTURE STACK

The ecosystem can broadly be divided into 9 sub-layers:

• Power Generation
• Power Transmission
• Power Equipment
• Data Centre Developers
• Data Centre Operators
• Data Centre Hardware
• Semiconductor OSAT
• Semiconductor Materials
• Semiconductor Hardware

This distinction matters.
AI does not simply require more servers.
It requires:
Electricity → generation capacity → transmission → substations → transformers → switchgear → cooling → data-centre buildings → networking/fibre → servers → semiconductors → packaging/testing → specialised materials.

Therefore, the economic opportunity can spread across the entire industrial supply chain.
Management commentary is already showing this change.
AI-related discussions have increased sharply, while earnings calls increasingly mention terms such as data centres, hyperscale, GPUs, transformers, switchgear, substations, power-purchase agreements, fibre infrastructure, OSAT and data lakes.
Importantly, these discussions are expanding beyond traditional technology companies into industrials, utilities, telecom and infrastructure companies.

The classification is based on exposure to the AI infrastructure supply chain rather than companies being pure-play AI businesses.

WHY POWER MAY BE THE REAL BOTTLENECK
The fundamental starting point is electricity.
AI data centres are significantly more power-intensive than conventional digital infrastructure.

That creates a multi-stage investment cycle:

More AI workloads → more data-centre capacity → higher electricity demand → additional generation → transmission investment → transformers/switchgear/substations → higher demand for electrical equipment.

This is why the opportunity extends from renewable power developers such as Adani Green Energy, Tata Power, NTPC Green Energy, ACME Solar and Clean Max to transmission companies such as Power Grid, Adani Energy Solutions and KEC International, and further into electrical equipment companies such as ABB India, Hitachi Energy India, GE Vernova T&D, Schneider Electric Infrastructure and TD Power Systems.

The key point is that AI capex can create second-order industrial demand even for companies with no direct AI revenue.

THE CAPEX CYCLE IS ACCELERATING
AI Enablers are entering a significant investment phase.
Consensus estimates in the report indicate:
AI Enabler capex growth:
2025: ~18%
2026E: ~65%
2027E: ~12%

The 2026 acceleration is particularly important because AI Enablers are expected to contribute around 6 percentage points of Nifty 500 aggregate capex growth.
The largest contributors to the capex cycle include power generation, power transmission, data-centre operators and semiconductor OSAT.
Yet the cohort is expected to remain free-cash-flow positive in aggregate, supported by strong revenue growth.
This creates an important fundamental distinction:
AI infrastructure is not just a demand story — it is also a capital-cycle story.

Investors need to track whether incremental capex translates into revenue, EBITDA and ultimately free cash flow.

EARNINGS ARE ALREADY SHOWING THE DIFFERENCE
Consensus expects AI Enabler earnings to grow:
CY26E: +53%
CY27E: +39%
CY28E: +29%

Against approximately 16% CY27E earnings growth for MSCI India.

All nine AI sub-layers are expected to grow faster than the Nifty 500.

The strongest projected CY27E growth pockets include:
Power Generation: ~62%
Data Centre Hardware: ~57%
AI Enablers overall: ~39%
Power Equipment: ~38%
And the earnings revision cycle is equally interesting.

CY27E EPS estimates for the overall AI Enabler cohort have been upgraded approximately 22% YTD in 2026, while Nifty 500 estimates have declined around 2%.

The biggest upgrade has come from:
Data Centre Hardware: +95%
Power Equipment: +15%
Semiconductor Materials: +8%
Power Transmission: +5%

However, the cycle is not uniformly positive across every sub-layer.
CY27E estimates have been cut for:

Data Centre Developers: -15%
Power Generation: -14%

That dispersion is important because “AI exposure” by itself does not guarantee earnings delivery.

STOCK-LEVEL FUNDAMENTALS SHOW HUGE DISPERSION
The 42-stock universe is far from homogeneous.

Examples :
NTPC Green Energy: CY27E earnings growth 106%; capex/sales 613%
ACME Solar: 86% earnings growth; 487% capex/sales

For example:

Power Grid: 8% CY27E earnings growth, 14% FCF/sales

This demonstrates that the AI infrastructure universe contains both high-growth capex plays and mature cash-generating infrastructure businesses.

THE MOST IMPORTANT FUNDAMENTAL VARIABLE: CAPEX INTENSITY
One of the strongest signals in the dataset is the enormous difference in capital intensity.

Companies such as NTPC Green Energy, ACME Solar, Adani Green and Clean Max have extremely high projected capex-to-sales ratios.

Meanwhile, equipment manufacturers such as ABB India, Siemens, Cummins and Schneider Electric Infrastructure can participate in the same capex cycle without necessarily deploying equivalent levels of capital themselves.

This creates two very different business models:

Infrastructure owners:
Higher capital requirements → large asset creation → potentially large revenue pools → but greater financing and cash-flow requirements.

Equipment suppliers:
Sell the infrastructure → participate in multiple projects → potentially higher capital efficiency.

That distinction is crucial when analysing AI infrastructure companies.

DATA-CENTRE HARDWARE IS ANOTHER KEY NODE

The data-centre hardware layer has emerged as one of the strongest earnings-revision pockets.

CY27E earnings estimates for the sub-layer were upgraded approximately 95% YTD.

Companies such as:

#Netweb Technologies
#Kaynes Technology
#CGPower
#Syrma SGS
#Sterlite Technologies
#HFCL
#Waaree Energies

provide exposure to different portions of the hardware, electronics, connectivity and semiconductor ecosystem.
The fundamental opportunity is that AI data centres require much more than computing chips.
They need:
Servers + networking + fibre + power systems + cooling + storage + racks + electronics + connectivity.

That broadens the addressable market considerably.

SEMICONDUCTORS: THE NEXT LAYER DOWN

India’s AI infrastructure opportunity also extends into semiconductor manufacturing and supporting materials.

The identified universe includes companies exposed to:

OSAT / semiconductor packaging
Semiconductor hardware
Specialised chemicals/materials

Names include:

CG Power
Gujarat Fluorochemicals
Navin Fluorine
Himadri Speciality Chemical
Kaynes Technology
Syrma SGS

The strategic importance is that semiconductor localisation requires an ecosystem rather than a single fabrication facility.

Packaging, testing, specialty chemicals, materials, electronics and supporting equipment can all become part of the domestic semiconductor supply chain.

THE TELECOM + FIBRE ANGLE
AI workloads also require massive data movement.

That brings companies such as Bharti Airtel, Reliance Industries, HFCL and Sterlite Technologies into the broader infrastructure discussion.

The AI stack therefore extends beyond electricity and servers into:

Fibre → network connectivity → data transmission → data centres → computing.

This is particularly relevant because AI infrastructure increasingly depends on low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity between data centres and users.

VALUATION IS WHERE THE FUNDAMENTAL DISCUSSION BECOMES IMPORTANT
The AI Enabler cohort trades at approximately 36x forward PE, around an 85% premium to MSCI India and near the upper end of its five-year valuation range.
However, the earnings-growth differential is substantial.

The cohort’s PEG ratio is approximately 1.3x versus 1.4x for MSCI India.

But valuation dispersion between sub-layers is enormous:

Semiconductor Hardware: ~66x
Power Equipment: ~48x
Semiconductor OSAT: ~45x
Semiconductor Materials: ~39x
AI Enablers: ~36x
Data Centre Hardware: ~35x
Power Generation: ~30x
Data Centre Operators: ~26x
Data Centre Developers: ~20x
Power Transmission: ~19x

So “AI exposure” should not be treated as a single valuation bucket.
The market is assigning very different multiples depending on growth, capital intensity, cash generation, competitive positioning and expected AI exposure.

THE BIG INVESTMENT TAKEAWAY
The most important insight is that India’s AI opportunity may not primarily be about finding the company selling the AI application.

It may be about identifying the physical bottlenecks required to make AI infrastructure possible.

Every incremental hyperscale data centre potentially creates demand for:

Power generation
Transmission
Transformers
Switchgear
Substations
Cooling
Fibre
Networking
Servers
Electronics
Semiconductor packaging
Specialty materials

That creates a potentially long industrial multiplier effect.

The 42-stock universe therefore represents a complete AI infrastructure ecosystem rather than a collection of AI-themed stocks.

But the fundamental work starts after identifying the theme.

Investors need to differentiate between:

Revenue growth vs AI-linked revenue
Capex growth vs productive capex
Order wins vs executable orders
Earnings growth vs cash-flow growth
Capacity expansion vs utilisation
High growth vs high capital intensity
AI exposure vs actual economic sensitivity to AI capex
Growth vs valuation

The biggest question for the next phase of the cycle is therefore not simply:

“Which companies are exposed to AI?”
It is:
“Which companies can convert the AI infrastructure capex cycle into sustainable revenue, margins, earnings and free cash flow without requiring ever-higher capital expenditure?”

That is where the fundamental differentiation within India’s AI infrastructure ecosystem is likely to emerge.
